chapter: Trummy Young's band, 52nd Street and the Navy
title: Draft notice after the Apollo week and his reluctance to serve
summary: Called up just after the band plays the Apollo, he explains why he felt he had no place in anybody's army.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: We stayed down there until about June, I believe. Then we went in and we did a week in the Apollo Theatre. I think right after that was when I got a message from home with some greetings that Uncle Sam had called me to go into the Armed Services. Which broke my heart! Because I was the last person in the world who felt like I wanted to go in the Armed Services and leave 52nd Street. Not only that, but for other reasons, I felt like I had no business in anybody's Army

fighting Germans or Japanese or anybody else who I'd never had no association with. Or, in fact, as a young man that I was then, thinking that way, I felt like if I was going in the Army, I should have been going down to Mississippi somewhere to fight somebody down there. At the same time, I knew that after the War was over, these same people that we were going over there to fight would come over here, and they would be doing everything from calling me a nigger to getting a better job than me or anything else. You know? So I just felt like I had no place in nobody's Army. Because to me, going in the Army meant that you were making a commitment to lay down you life for something, and that just didn't make sense to me. With my optimism about being a musician and looking forward to everything at that particular time, the height of what... I really saw that things were really opening up to where I had really begun to feel like a musician. Before then, it had been something I was doing. But it hadn't been too long that I had committed myself to being a professional musician.
